html:
The flight and forced removal of some 12 million Germans from Central and Eastern Europe between 1944 and 1950, at the end of and after the Second World War. It is often called the largest forced move in European history.

In late 1944 and early 1945, as the Red Army advanced, millions of Germans fled west from East Prussia, Silesia and Pomerania. After Germany's defeat, the Allies moved Poland's border west to the Oder and Neisse rivers, and the Potsdam Conference of 1945 approved the "orderly and humane" transfer of the Germans left in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary. In practice many removals were brutal, especially the first "wild" expulsions.

Many families had lived in these lands for centuries. Estimates of how many died vary widely and are disputed, from about half a million to two million.

The refugees were settled in what became West and East Germany. The expulsions came after the Nazi war of conquest, the Holocaust and mass killing in occupied Eastern Europe, and they remain a painful and political subject.
sum: The flight and forced removal of some 12 million Germans from Central and Eastern Europe between 1944 and 1950, at the end of and after the Second World War. It is often called the largest forced move in European history.
